How does Nevada decide what a house is worth for tax?

Nevada property tax starts with the county assessor, an elected official who finds, lists and values the real and personal property in the county, according to the Nevada Department of Taxation's guide to the property tax. The state department oversees the system, but the number on your bill begins at the county level.

The state describes taxable value as the full cash value of the land plus the replacement cost new, less depreciation, of the improvements. For a house, that means the lot is valued on what it would sell for, and the building is valued on what it would cost to rebuild today minus a depreciation allowance for age and wear. That is a different method from a sale price, so an assessor's figure and an offer on your house can differ.

The assessed value is a fraction of that taxable value. NRS 361.225 requires all taxable property to be assessed at 35 percent of its taxable value. A notice of assessed value goes to each owner at the same time the tax roll is prepared.

  • Land: full cash value, which is close to market value for the lot.
  • Improvements: replacement cost new, minus depreciation.
  • Assessed value: 35 percent of the sum of the two.
  • Tax bill: assessed value multiplied by the combined local rate, then reduced by any abatement.

Is there a cap on how much Nevada property tax can rise?

Yes. Two limits apply: a ceiling on the total tax rate, and an abatement that holds down year-over-year increases on homes.

NRS 361.453 sets the total ad valorem levy for all public purposes at no more than $3.64 on each $100 of assessed valuation, with listed exceptions. The Department of Taxation notes the Legislature set that rate in 1979 and added $0.02 for state debt, which brings the total to $3.66. As a ceiling calculation only, a house with an assessed value of $140,000 would top out near $5,096 a year at $3.64 per $100 before any abatement (1,400 units of $100 times $3.64). Your actual rate depends on where the parcel sits, so look at your bill.

The abatement is in NRS 361.4723. The Legislature there found that a bill rising more than 3 percent over the prior year is a hardship, and it directs a partial abatement for an owner-occupied single-family residence. The department's guide describes the effect: the tax bill on these dwellings cannot rise more than 3 percent over the prior year's levy. Other parcels fall under a general abatement that the department describes as reaching up to 8 percent.

ItemWhat the source saysSource
Assessment ratio35 percent of taxable valueNRS 361.225
Total levy ceiling$3.64 per $100 of assessed value, with exceptionsNRS 361.453
Primary residence abatementBill cannot rise more than 3 percent over the prior yearNRS 361.4723
Other parcelsGeneral abatement, described as up to 8 percentDepartment of Taxation guide

When are Nevada property taxes due, and what are the late penalties?

Taxes on the real property roll are due on the third Monday of August, and an owner may pay in four roughly equal installments if the bill is more than $100 (NRS 361.483).

Under that statute the installment dates are the third Monday of August, the first Monday of October, the first Monday of January and the first Monday of March. County treasurers report the same pattern. The Nye County treasurer says bills are prepared and mailed by August 1, for example.

  • One installment unpaid 10 days after its due date: 4 percent penalty.
  • Two installments unpaid: 5 percent on the two installments due.
  • Three installments unpaid: 6 percent on the three installments due.
  • Full amount unpaid 10 days after the first Monday of March: 7 percent of the full amount.

The statute also tells the county tax receiver to notify anyone who is penalized about the waiver provisions in NRS 361.4835. That section lets a county treasurer or assessor waive all or part of a late-payment penalty and interest in the circumstances it describes, so ask the treasurer before assuming a penalty is final.

What happens to a Nevada house when the taxes are not paid?

The tax stays attached to the property. Under NRS 361.450, every property tax is a perpetual lien until paid, and it is superior to all other liens, claims, encumbrances and titles on the property, whether or not the other lien was filed or perfected first. The lien attaches on July 1 of the year the taxes are levied.

If the bill is still open after the first Monday in June, the Clark County Treasurer explains that the county must hold the property for a two-year redemption period, during which the owner can redeem by paying the taxes, penalties, costs and 10 percent annual interest. If nothing is paid, the property is deeded to the county treasurer as trustee and can be sold at public auction. The Nevada tax sale guide on this site covers that process in detail.

Two practical points follow from the lien rules. First, a buyer or title company will treat unpaid tax as something that has to be cleared at closing. Second, a short delay costs real money, because the penalty ladder above and the interest after a certificate both add up month by month.

What should a Nevada seller check on the tax side before listing?

Start with three documents: the latest tax bill, the notice of assessed value, and the county treasurer's account page showing whether any installment is open.

  1. Confirm which installments are paid and which are due. A balance can sit open for months without the owner noticing if the bill went to an old mailing address or to a lender.
  2. Check whether the abatement applies. The residence has to be the owner's designated primary residence and cannot be rented or made available for exclusive occupancy by anyone other than the owner and family (NRS 361.4723).
  3. Compare the assessor's figures with reality. A county board appeal under NRS 361.357 cannot raise your taxable value, and the filing deadline is January 15. The owner must first complete the assessor's form.
  4. Ask whether special assessments are attached. NRS 361.450 treats assessments under chapter 271 as liens with the same priority as tax.

Owners of inherited houses should also find out who is on the tax roll. If the former owner has died and the bill still goes to their address, delinquency can build before anyone notices.

What transfer tax applies when a Nevada house sells?

Nevada charges a real property transfer tax on each deed, and the rate depends on county size. NRS 375.020 sets $1.25 for each $500 of value in a county with 700,000 or more people, and 65 cents for each $500 in a smaller county, when the value of what is conveyed exceeds $100.

The tax is computed on the value declared on the declaration of value form required by NRS 375.060. For a $400,000 sale, that works out to 800 units of $500: $1,000 at the higher rate and $520 at the lower rate. Check with the county recorder for any additional local charges, because this statute section covers only the base tax.

Who pays is a contract term, so the purchase agreement should say. In a typical sale the transfer tax, prorated property tax and any open delinquency all appear on the settlement statement.

Can I sell a Nevada house with property tax owing?

Yes. A house with tax owing can sell, as long as the title company can clear the lien at closing, usually by paying the balance from the sale proceeds.

Cash buyers handle this often because they do not depend on a lender's underwriting timeline. The practical steps are the same either way: get a payoff figure from the county treasurer, include penalties and interest to the closing date, and give the escrow officer enough time to confirm the amount. If a trustee certificate has already been issued, the redemption cost is higher, since it includes interest at 10 percent a year plus costs.

Timing matters most when the house is close to an auction. Nevada law lets an owner, a lender and a person holding a contract to purchase redeem until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale (NRS 361.585). A buyer under contract can therefore protect the deal, but only if the money moves in time. We make offers on Nevada houses as-is, and we can review a tax bill with you before you decide anything.

More questions about Nevada Property Tax Guide

Who sets my Nevada property tax rate?

Several local bodies do, within the state ceiling. The total levy for all public purposes cannot exceed $3.64 per $100 of assessed value except as the statute allows (NRS 361.453). The county assessor sets the value and the county treasurer sends the bill.

What is the assessed value of a Nevada house?

It is 35 percent of taxable value, under NRS 361.225. Taxable value is the land's full cash value plus the replacement cost of improvements less depreciation, per the Nevada Department of Taxation.

Can I pay Nevada property tax in installments?

Yes, if the bill is over $100. The four installments are due the third Monday of August, then the first Mondays of October, January and March (NRS 361.483). Penalties start at 4 percent for one late installment.

Does a tax lien come ahead of other liens in Nevada?

Yes. NRS 361.450 says the property tax lien is superior to all other liens, claims and encumbrances on the property, whether or not the other lien was filed first.

Is there a limit on how much my Nevada home tax can increase?

For an owner-occupied single-family primary residence, the partial abatement in NRS 361.4723 holds the yearly increase to 3 percent. Other property has a general abatement that the Department of Taxation describes as up to 8 percent.

What does the Nevada homestead exemption actually protect?

The homestead exemption protects a home from a forced sale to pay most creditors, up to a set amount of equity. Under NRS 115.010, the homestead is not subject to forced sale on execution or any final court process, and the protection extends only to equity of $605,000 unless allodial title has been established and not relinquished.

This is a creditor-protection rule, and it is separate from property tax relief. NRS 115.080 says nothing in the chapter exempts property from sale for taxes. Owners who want a lower tax bill should look at the abatement and exemption programs covered further down.

Equity has its own definition in the statute. It is the fair market value of the property minus the liens that the homestead exemption does not protect against, including mortgages and certain other liens. A house worth $700,000 with a $200,000 mortgage has $500,000 of equity under that formula, which sits inside the $605,000 limit. That is an illustration of the formula, not a statement about any particular property.

What counts as a homestead in Nevada?

A homestead can be land with a dwelling and its appurtenances, a mobile home whether or not the claimant owns the land under it, or a condominium or common-interest unit with its share of common elements. NRS 115.005 gives those three categories, and the claim is made by both spouses, either spouse, or a single person.

The declaration for a married claimant must say the claimants are married and live on the premises with their family or with the people they support. For anyone, it must state an intention to use and claim the property as a homestead. If the property is the separate property of one spouse, both spouses must join in signing and acknowledging the declaration.

Tenants in common may each declare a homestead in their own share, subject to the rights of their co-owners to force a partition, according to NRS 115.030. A trustee can claim a homestead for the person who created the trust, or for beneficiaries, when those people live in the property.

How do you file a Nevada homestead declaration?

You sign the declaration, have it acknowledged, and record it with the county recorder in the county where the property sits. The statute requires the same acknowledgment and recording as a deed.

The Real Estate Division of the Department of Business and Industry prescribes a form, and NRS 115.025 says it must be free at the Division's offices and website and at each county recorder's office. Using the form is optional, but it carries the required statements.

  • Pick the property you actually live in and describe it in the declaration.
  • Sign it, and have the signature acknowledged before a notary.
  • Record it with the county recorder. The recorder may charge a recording fee, and the statute says a declaration can otherwise be recorded without a fee.
  • Keep a certified copy with your closing and estate papers.

There is a consumer warning built into the law. A person who solicits you and charges a fee for recording your declaration must first hand you a bold-type notice saying you can record it yourself, and a violation is a misdemeanor under NRS 115.020.

What debts can still reach a homestead?

Several kinds of claims are outside the exemption. NRS 115.010 says the protection does not extend to process to enforce the debt for buying the property, for improvements to it including a mechanic's lien, for legal taxes, or for a mortgage or deed of trust, including a second mortgage, refinance, line of credit or home equity loan.

Association liens are also covered. A lien to which the owner gave prior consent by accepting property subject to recorded restrictions, which the statute says specifically includes an association lien under NRS 116.3116 or 117.070, is outside the exemption. NRS 115.090 adds that nothing in the chapter blocks recovery of money owed to the Nevada Health Authority for Medicaid benefits through a lien.

ClaimReaches a homestead?Statute
General unsecured judgmentProtected up to $605,000 of equityNRS 115.010
Mortgage, deed of trust, HELOCYesNRS 115.010
Purchase price or improvement debt, mechanic's lienYesNRS 115.010
Property taxesYesNRS 115.010, 115.080
Association lienYesNRS 115.010
Medicaid recovery lienYesNRS 115.090

Allodial title changes some of this, since the statute then extends the exemption to those debts unless a waiver was signed. That route is rare and has its own rules, so get legal advice before relying on it.

Can you sell a homestead, and who has to sign?

Yes. A homestead can be sold, and the exemption does not stop the owner from conveying it. The signature rules are what trip people up. NRS 115.040 says a mortgage or alienation made to secure a loan is not valid unless both spouses sign and acknowledge it, when the relationship exists.

A homestead is also not treated as abandoned without a written declaration of abandonment, signed and acknowledged by both spouses or by the single claimant and recorded in the same office as the original declaration. If an owner moves out and wants the claim off the record, that is the document to record.

If a spouse cannot join because of incapacity, NRS 115.070 lets the owner petition the district court for a license to convey by the owner's sole deed, on at least 20 days' notice to the spouse's kindred living in the state. The court can also direct how the proceeds are invested to protect the spouse.

If a declaration is on record, tell the escrow officer early so the abandonment and signature questions are settled before the closing date.

What happens to sale proceeds under the homestead law?

In a forced sale, the first $605,000 goes to the homeowner, and that money keeps protection only if it is reinvested quickly. NRS 115.050 describes the case where a creditor swears that equity exceeds $605,000 and the court appoints three appraisers. If the property cannot be divided, it is sold, no bid under $605,000 may be accepted, and $605,000 is paid to the debtor.

NRS 115.055 then sets the clock for that money. It is exempt from execution only if it is reinvested in another property of like kind for which a homestead will be declared, and the new property must be identified within 45 days after the sale of the homestead and possessed within 180 days.

These deadlines are written for the execution-sale setting. An ordinary voluntary sale to a buyer is a different situation, so ask an attorney how the rule applies to your facts before you treat the 45 and 180 day dates as your own.

How does the homestead pass when an owner dies?

For a declared homestead held as community property, the couple is treated as holding it with a right of survivorship, and on the first death the property vests in the survivor. NRS 115.060 adds that the exemption continues without a new filing as to debts existing against the spouses until the death of the survivor.

For a single owner, the exemption continues as to debts existing at death and as to later debts of a relative by blood or marriage who lived in the house and keeps living there. NRS 146.010 separately lets a surviving spouse or minor children stay in possession of the homestead, and NRS 146.020 allows a court to set it apart. A homestead selected and recorded by the spouses during their marriage vests absolutely in the survivor under NRS 146.050 unless NRS 115.060 requires otherwise.

Heirs who want to sell an inherited house should read our probate guide, because letters or a court order may be needed first.

What property tax relief is separate from the homestead exemption?

Nevada limits the yearly increase in tax on a primary residence through a partial abatement. NRS 361.4723 applies a 3 percent cap, and the Clark County Assessor says only one property in the state can be the chosen primary residence. A cap of up to 8 percent applies to homes that are not owner occupied.

The Department of Taxation also lists exemptions for veterans, disabled veterans, surviving spouses and blind persons, claimed through the county assessor. Taxes themselves are due in four installments on the third Monday of August, first Monday of October, first Monday of January and first Monday of March, and the Department says you can appeal an assessment to the County Board of Equalization, usually in January.

A seller who is behind on taxes should know the homestead does not protect against a tax sale. Paying from sale proceeds at closing is often the cleanest fix, and the escrow officer will order the balance from the county.

More questions about Nevada Homestead Exemption

How much is the Nevada homestead exemption?

It protects up to $605,000 of equity under NRS 115.010, unless allodial title has been established and not relinquished. The figure applies to equity after the liens that the exemption does not protect against, not to the home's market value.

Is the Nevada homestead exemption a property tax break?

No. It protects the home from forced sale to creditors, and NRS 115.080 says the chapter does not exempt property from sale for taxes. Property tax relief comes from the 3 percent abatement and the veteran, surviving spouse and similar exemptions.

Do I have to file a homestead declaration in Nevada?

The statute describes the protection as arising from a declaration that is signed, acknowledged and recorded with the county recorder. The Real Estate Division's form is free at the Division and each county recorder, and you can record it yourself.

Can a spouse refuse to sign when I sell a homestead?

A mortgage or other alienation to secure a debt on a homestead is invalid without both spouses' signatures under NRS 115.040. When one spouse cannot join because of incapacity, NRS 115.070 provides a court license to convey by the owner's sole deed.

Does the homestead protect my house from a mortgage foreclosure?

No. NRS 115.010 says the exemption does not reach a mortgage or deed of trust, including second mortgages, refinances, lines of credit and home equity loans. It also does not reach purchase money debt, mechanic's liens, taxes or association liens.

Should I record an abandonment before selling?

If a homestead declaration is on record and you are leaving, NRS 115.040 says the homestead is not abandoned without a recorded written declaration signed and acknowledged by both spouses or the single claimant. Ask the title company whether one is needed for your sale.

What does Nevada call a transfer on death deed?

Nevada's statutes call it a deed upon death. NRS 111.671 lets the owner of an interest in property convey it to one beneficiary or several, with the deed taking effect only when the owner dies. The rules sit in NRS 111.655 to 111.699.

The statute gives a model form in NRS 111.695. Its wording tells you most of what you need to know: the deed is revocable, it transfers no ownership until the grantor dies, and it revokes all earlier deeds upon death for the same real property. It must be signed, notarized and recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies, or it does nothing.

Because the form lists the county, city and legal description of the property, the safest approach is to copy those details from your current vesting deed. A typo in the legal description is the kind of problem that shows up years later, when the beneficiary tries to sell.

What can an owner still do while alive?

Nearly everything. NRS 111.685 says that during the owner's lifetime a deed upon death does not affect the owner's rights, including the right to transfer or encumber the property. The beneficiary gets no legal or equitable interest while the owner is alive.

The same section lists other effects the deed does not have:

  • It does not affect any other permitted method of transferring the property.
  • It does not reduce the rights of the owner's secured or unsecured creditors, even if they know about it.
  • It does not affect the owner's or the beneficiary's eligibility for public assistance.
  • It does not expose the property to claims by the beneficiary's creditors.

Two statutes cover changes of plan. Under NRS 111.677, if the owner transfers the property to someone else during life, the deed upon death is void. If the owner records more than one deed upon death for the same property, the last one recorded before death is the effective deed. That makes a new recorded deed a practical way to change beneficiaries.

What must happen after the owner dies?

The beneficiary must record a Death of Grantor Affidavit. NRS 111.699 says that on the death of the last grantor, a declaration of value (the form under NRS 375.060) and a copy of each grantor's death certificate must be attached to the affidavit and recorded in the office of the county recorder where the deed was recorded.

The affidavit identifies the deceased as the person named in the deed, gives the recording details of the deed and the property description, and states that the signer is a beneficiary or the beneficiary's authorized representative. It must be sworn before a notary.

Recording matters for a sale. Under NRS 111.689(9), a person who deals in good faith and for valuable consideration with a beneficiary has the same protections as if the beneficiary had been named in a final order of distribution, provided the Death of Grantor Affidavit was recorded. Without that recording, a buyer or title company has less to rely on.

StepWho actsSource
Sign, notarize and record the deedOwner, before deathNRS 111.695, 111.681
Record Death of Grantor Affidavit with death certificate and declaration of valueBeneficiaryNRS 111.699
Publish notice to creditors and mail it to listed partiesBeneficiaryNRS 111.689
Wait for the claim period, then sell or distributeBeneficiaryNRS 111.689

Do creditors and Medicaid still have a claim against a Nevada deed upon death?

Yes. A deed upon death avoids probate for that property, but it does not erase debts. NRS 111.689 says that if the grantor's probate estate cannot cover an allowed claim or a statutory allowance to a surviving spouse or child, the estate may enforce the liability against property that passed by the deed.

The statute puts the notice job on the beneficiary. After the death, the beneficiary must publish a notice to creditors and mail a copy to the grantor's personal representative if known, the Department of Health and Human Services, and known or readily ascertainable creditors. A creditor then has 90 days after mailing or after the first publication to file a claim with the beneficiary, and a late claim is barred.

The Department has its own track. If it receives notice, it must tell the beneficiary within 45 days whether the grantor received public assistance and, if not, give an original waiver of claim for recording. If the beneficiary never gives notice, the property stays subject to the Department's right to recover assistance, and NRS 111.693 adds that the deed statutes do not limit Medicaid recovery.

When a creditor claim is rejected, the beneficiary has 10 days to send written notice by registered or certified mail, and the claimant then has 30 days to sue or the claim is barred.

Can a beneficiary sell the house after the owner dies?

Yes, and many do. Once the claim period has run, NRS 111.689(5) lets the beneficiaries sell or distribute the property without personal liability for claims that were not timely filed, as long as they gave written notice to the Department of Health and Human Services and received the waiver of claim the statute describes.

That clause turns the order of tasks into a checklist for anyone planning a sale:

  1. Record the Death of Grantor Affidavit with the death certificate and declaration of value.
  2. Publish the creditor notice and mail it to the required parties, including the Department.
  3. Wait out the 90 day claim window and the Department's 45 day response.
  4. Give the title company copies of the recorded documents. The statute says a title company may treat the notices as adequate notice and is not liable for claims it was not told about.
  5. Sign the sale deed. A sale to a buyer is a regular conveyance, so the transfer tax in NRS 375.020 applies at $1.25 per $500 of value in a county of 700,000 or more people and 65 cents per $500 in a smaller county.

If the beneficiaries do not want the house, NRS 111.687 allows a beneficiary to disclaim all or part of the interest by recording a disclaimer with the county recorder under chapter 120.

What if the deed is missing, defective or has several beneficiaries?

The statutes provide no shortcut around a bad deed. An unrecorded deed does not work, a void deed does not work, and a deed with a wrong legal description invites a title dispute. In those cases the property may have to go through probate instead. Our Nevada probate guide explains that path.

Several beneficiaries bring a separate problem. All of them hold title once the deed takes effect, so a sale needs their agreement and signatures. If one beneficiary lives out of state, is hard to reach or disagrees about price, the sale slows down quickly.

  • Check that the deed was recorded before death and that the recording details match the affidavit.
  • Gather death certificates for every grantor, not only the last to die.
  • Make a list of every beneficiary and a way to contact each one.
  • Ask the title company early what it will require.

We buy inherited Nevada houses as-is, including houses that still hold the owner's belongings or need repairs. Because we pay cash, there is no lender appraisal to hold up closing once the paperwork is in order.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

More questions about Nevada Transfer on Death Deed

What is the difference between a deed upon death and a will in Nevada?

A recorded deed upon death passes the named property directly to the beneficiary when the owner dies, while a will usually goes through probate. The deed only works for real property it describes, and it must be recorded before death (NRS 111.671).

Can I sell my house after recording a deed upon death in Nevada?

Yes. The deed does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property during life (NRS 111.685). A transfer during life makes the deed void under NRS 111.677.

Does a Nevada deed upon death avoid creditors?

No. If the probate estate is insufficient, the estate can enforce liabilities against the property, and the beneficiary must publish and mail a creditor notice. Creditors have 90 days to file claims (NRS 111.689).

What document does a beneficiary record after death in Nevada?

A Death of Grantor Affidavit, with a declaration of value and a death certificate for each grantor, recorded with the county recorder where the deed was recorded (NRS 111.699).

Can a beneficiary refuse a Nevada deed upon death?

Yes. NRS 111.687 allows a beneficiary to disclaim all or part of the interest by recording a disclaimer with the county recorder.

Nevada Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale

Cash Home Buyers in Nevada

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Nevada Tax Sales sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Nevada?

How does a Nevada tax sale work from missed payment to auction?

A Nevada tax sale is the last step of a county process that starts with an unpaid bill and runs through a two-year redemption period, a deed to the county treasurer and a public sale. The owner keeps the right to pay and stop the process at nearly every stage.

The lien comes first. NRS 361.450 makes every property tax a perpetual lien that attaches on July 1 of the tax year and ranks ahead of other liens. When installments go unpaid, the tax receiver publishes and mails delinquency notices under NRS 361.5648 and 361.565, then issues a certificate for each unpaid property. Under NRS 361.570, that certificate lets the county treasurer, acting as trustee for the State and county, hold the property for 2 years after the first Monday in June of the certificate year, unless it is redeemed sooner.

StageWhat happensSource
July 1Tax lien attaches to the propertyNRS 361.450
Third Monday of August onwardTaxes due; installments follow in October, January and MarchNRS 361.483
First Monday in JuneDelinquent property goes onto a certificate held by the treasurer as trusteeNRS 361.570; Clark County Treasurer
Two years laterRedemption period ends; deed goes to the treasurer in trustNRS 361.570, 361.585
After the deedCounty commissioners can order a sale; notice by certified mail at least 90 days aheadNRS 361.595

How long do I have to redeem my Nevada property?

The base period is two years from the date of the certificate, and during it the owner can redeem by paying everything owed. The Clark County Treasurer states that the redemption payment includes the taxes, accruing taxes, penalties and costs, plus interest on the taxes at 10 percent per year from the original due date.

NRS 361.570 adds a point that surprises owners: the property keeps being assessed during the redemption period. Before redeeming, the owner must also pay taxes, penalties and costs that accrue after the certificate date, with the same 10 percent interest, assessed monthly. The payoff therefore grows each year.

There is a shorter path for abandoned property. Under NRS 361.567 the tax receiver may use an expedited procedure for property found to be abandoned, and the certificate then gives only 1 year of redemption. Clark County's treasurer notes that this election is available after a one year period for such properties.

  • Normal certificate: 2 years to redeem.
  • Abandoned property under the expedited procedure: 1 year.
  • Notice by certified mail before a trustee sale: at least 90 days, or at least 45 days in the expedited case (NRS 361.595).

Can I still get my property back after the deed goes to the county?

Yes, for a short window. Even after the county treasurer holds the deed as trustee, NRS 361.585 lets certain people have the property reconveyed by paying the taxes, costs, penalties and interest, until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale. The Washoe County Treasurer repeats this deadline on its auction page and adds that the treasurer may withdraw a property before or at the auction.

The statute does not limit reconveyance to the owner. The people who may redeem include:

  • The owner and the person to whom the property was assessed.
  • A beneficiary under a deed of trust or a mortgagee.
  • A judgment creditor.
  • A person holding a contract to purchase the property before it was conveyed to the county treasurer.
  • The Director of the Department of Health and Human Services if the owner has received Medicaid benefits.
  • A municipality that holds a lien, and any successor in interest.

The purchase-contract line matters to sellers. A buyer who signed a contract before the deed to the treasurer can pay what is owed and take the property back out of trust. A lender or a family member with a recorded interest has similar rights.

How do Nevada counties actually run the auction?

Each county treasurer runs its own sale, so the format and calendar vary. Washoe County says it holds one real estate tax auction a year, usually in April, and lists the next one as April 2027. Bidders register before the sale, and the treasurer records a quitclaim deed within 30 days of the auction.

The opening bid is set by the county. Washoe explains that it is the delinquent taxes, assessments, costs, interest and penalties, or the assessed valuation, whichever is greater. The assessed value is about 35 percent of appraised value, so in some cases it exceeds the tax debt. The county says its sole interest is to recover what is owed and that buyers must investigate the property for themselves.

Nye County lists 2026 online-only tax sale auctions, and the Clark County Treasurer publishes a trustee auction parcel list that it updates often, with some parcels crossed out when they are no longer eligible. Those pages show how quickly a parcel can drop off the list when someone pays.

NRS 361.595 sets the sale notice rules. Notice must be posted in at least three public places, including the courthouse and the property, at least 20 days ahead, or published for four weeks. Separately, the owner and any lienholders of record get certified mail at least 90 days before the sale. The buyer receives a quitclaim deed, and the treasurer records it at the buyer's expense.

What happens to the money if the property sells for more than the tax debt?

The surplus belongs to the former owner or lienholders, but only if someone claims it in time. NRS 361.610 sets the order of payment, and a missed deadline sends the money to the county.

  1. The treasurer pays the taxes and costs on that parcel first.
  2. From the excess, the county general fund takes the first $300 and 10 percent of the next $10,000.
  3. The remainder goes into a separate interest-bearing account.
  4. A written claim must be made within 1 year after the treasurer's deed is recorded. After that, the money goes to the county general fund and cannot be refunded to the former owner.

The treasurer must approve or deny a claim within 30 days after the claim period ends. Lienholders such as lenders and certain associations rank ahead of the owner in the payment order. If more than one person claims, the matter goes to mediation, then to a hearing or an interpleader action. An aggrieved person has 90 days to seek judicial review in district court.

Be careful with people who offer to recover surplus funds for a fee. A recovery agreement must be in writing and signed, and for a natural person's primary residence the fee cannot exceed 10 percent of the remaining excess proceeds.

Can a city or county take the property without a sale?

In some cases, yes. NRS 361.603 lets a local government or the Nevada System of Higher Education apply to the board of county commissioners to acquire property held in trust, if a public purpose is served. The treasurer then sends notice of intent to sell to the last known owner or heirs.

The owner has 90 days after that notice to redeem by paying the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs. If the owner does not, the treasurer transfers the property to the local government for the amount of the delinquent taxes. When the transfer is for street, sewer or drainage use, for a program to rehabilitate abandoned residential properties, or for open space, the delinquent taxes need not be paid at all.

The 90 day notice goes to the last known owner or heirs, so an outdated mailing address is a real risk. Keep the treasurer's records current if you own a house you are not living in.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How can I sell a Nevada house before the tax sale?

The cleanest way is to close a sale while the property is still in your name or in redemption, and pay the county from the proceeds. Because the tax lien outranks other liens, a title company will require the balance cleared before it insures a buyer.

A cash purchase can move on a shorter clock than a financed one, since it avoids a lender appraisal and underwriting. The sequence is straightforward:

  • Ask the county treasurer for a written payoff figure, with the interest and costs through your expected closing date.
  • Find out whether the property is still in the redemption period or already deeded to the treasurer as trustee, because the deadline and the people who can redeem differ.
  • Sign the purchase contract and date it clearly, because the redemption right for a contract holder applies to a contract made before the property was conveyed to the treasurer.
  • Close, pay the treasurer, and collect what is left of your equity.

If the sale price is above the debt, you keep the difference. At auction, the surplus claim process described above applies instead, with a one year claim limit and county fees taken off first. We buy Nevada houses as-is and will give you a straight read on whether the timeline can work.

More questions about Nevada Tax Sales

What does a Nevada county tax sale sell?

It sells property that the county treasurer holds in trust after the redemption period ends. The treasurer delivers a quitclaim deed to the buyer under NRS 361.595, and the county's goal is to recover the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs.

Can I stop a Nevada tax sale by paying?

Yes. Under NRS 361.585 the owner and certain others can have the property reconveyed by paying the taxes, costs, penalties and interest until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale.

How much interest accrues on delinquent Nevada property tax?

NRS 361.570 states interest on the taxes accrues at 10 percent per year, assessed monthly, from the date due until paid. The Clark County Treasurer describes the same rate.

Do I get money if my Nevada house sells at a tax auction for more than I owed?

Possibly. After taxes and costs, the county takes the first $300 and 10 percent of the next $10,000, and the rest is held for claims. A written claim must be filed within 1 year after the deed is recorded (NRS 361.610).

Is the Nevada tax sale redemption period always two years?

No. The certificate allows 2 years to redeem, but NRS 361.570 gives only 1 year for property determined to be abandoned under the expedited procedure in NRS 361.567.

Does Nevada have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

Nevada has an estate tax on its books, but it collects nothing on deaths after 2004. NRS 375A.100 imposes a tax on the transfer of a taxable estate equal to the maximum credit allowed against the federal estate tax for state death taxes. That is a "pickup" tax, which depends entirely on the federal credit.

The Nevada Department of Taxation says filing is required only for a decedent who had Nevada property and died on or before December 31, 2004, with an estate large enough to require a federal estate tax return. For a death on or after January 1, 2005, Nevada does not require an estate tax filing and will not until the IRS re-enacts the death tax credit that existed before that date.

The Department's estate tax page describes only the NRS 375A tax.

What about the federal estate tax?

The federal estate tax is the one that can still matter. The IRS lists a filing threshold of $15,000,000 for a 2026 year of death, set by the 2025 tax law and indexed for inflation afterward. The Congressional Research Service notes that the exemption was $13.99 million in 2025.

An estate under that amount has no federal estate tax to pay. An estate over the threshold should work with a probate attorney and a CPA before any sale, since the federal return can affect how the sale proceeds are handled.

Nevada estate tax at a glance

ItemWhat the official source says
State estate tax lawNRS 375A.100, equal to the federal credit for state death taxes
State filing, deaths on or before December 31, 2004Required if the estate met the federal return level
State filing, deaths on or after January 1, 2005Not required
Federal filing threshold, 2026 death$15,000,000
Small estate set aside without administrationEstate not over $150,000 (NRS 146)
Transfer tax on a sale$1.95 per $500 of value, plus county add-ons
Department of Taxation phone(775) 684-2000
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

If the old Nevada estate tax applied, what were the rules?

For an estate that did owe the Nevada tax, the statute is strict, and it is relevant to a house sold years later. The tax was due on the date of the decedent's death and became delinquent nine months after that. The personal representative pays it from assets under his or her control, and the liability continues until it is paid.

The statute adds several consequences:

  • The tax becomes a lien on the gross estate on the date of death and remains until the tax, interest and penalties are paid or the lien is discharged.
  • If the tax is not paid when due, the person who held the property of the gross estate at death is personally liable.
  • A late return carries a penalty of 5% of the tax per month, up to 25%.
  • The lien does not attach to property sold to a bona fide purchaser or a holder of a security interest, but it follows the sale proceeds.
  • The Department can start collection within 10 years after a determination of deficiency is issued.

These rules matter only for the narrow group of pre-2005 deaths. If a title company flags an old Nevada estate tax lien on an inherited house, a payoff or release from the Department of Taxation will be needed before the sale can close.

What do heirs pay when they sell an inherited Nevada house?

The tax that usually applies is the Real Property Transfer Tax, collected by the County Recorder when the deed is recorded. In every county the rate is $1.95 for each $500 of value, and Washoe and Churchill counties add $0.10 while Clark County adds $0.60. The Department's example for a $100,500 transfer in Clark County is $514.50 total.

Both buyer and seller are liable for it together and individually, so the sale contract should say who pays. A Declaration of Value must accompany the deed. The Department lists 14 exemptions, and several matter to families:

  • A transfer without consideration to the remaining joint tenant or tenant in common.
  • A transfer between persons related within the first degree of lineal consanguinity or affinity.
  • A transfer to or from a trust without consideration, if a certificate of trust is present.
  • A deed upon death that becomes effective at the grantor's death under NRS 111.109.

A sale by heirs to an outside buyer is a transfer for value, so it is taxed even if the earlier transfer from the decedent was exempt. Heirs should also expect property tax to keep running while the estate is open.

Do heirs need probate before selling a house in Nevada?

It depends on how the house was titled. A recorded deed upon death avoids probate for that property, while a house in a sole name without one usually goes through court before it can be sold.

Under Nevada's real property transfer on death law, a deed upon death takes effect only at the owner's death, can be revoked while the owner is alive, and must be recorded before death. If the owner records more than one, the last one recorded before death controls. After the grantor's death, the beneficiary records an affidavit of death with the required documents. The beneficiary takes the property subject to any liens that existed on the date of death, and the statute provides a process for notifying creditors and filing claims.

Two other statutes affect an estate with real property:

  • NRS 146 allows an estate not over $150,000 to be set aside without administration by court order. The faster affidavit route for collecting property after 40 days is limited to estates that include no real property, as the DMV form summarizing NRS 146.080 states.
  • NRS 143 governs a personal representative's powers. The statutory notice form warns that a representative with limited authority has no authority, without court supervision, to sell or exchange real property.

Because the details turn on the estate, a Nevada probate attorney should confirm which path applies before a closing date is set.

How does a cash sale help an estate?

A cash sale can shorten the time an estate carries a vacant house. Cash Home Buyers purchases Nevada houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to the seller, and the offer is written. If an unpaid property tax installment or an old lien appears on title, the title company pays it from proceeds. Confirm statutes and amounts with the Nevada Department of Taxation, the County Recorder and your attorney, since this is general information, not legal or tax advice.

More questions about Nevada Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Nevada charge an estate tax?

Not currently in practice. NRS 375A.100 sets a tax equal to the federal credit for state death taxes, but the Department of Taxation says no Nevada filing is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

Does Nevada have an inheritance tax?

We found none in the Department of Taxation's estate tax page or the NRS 375A chapter. The only state death tax described there is the NRS 375A estate tax, which is not being collected.

What is the federal estate tax threshold for 2026?

The IRS lists $15,000,000 as the filing threshold for a 2026 year of death. Estates below that amount owe no federal estate tax.

Do heirs pay transfer tax when selling an inherited house in Nevada?

Generally yes if the house is sold to a buyer. The statewide rate is $1.95 per $500 of value, with $0.60 added in Clark County, and buyer and seller share liability. Some transfers, such as a deed upon death, are exempt.

Can I sell an inherited Nevada house without probate?

Possibly. A recorded deed upon death passes the property without probate. Otherwise a small estate up to $150,000 can be set aside by court order, and larger estates usually need a personal representative.

Who do I call about Nevada estate tax questions?

The Nevada Department of Taxation at (775) 684-2000. For transfer tax on a sale, call the County Recorder where the house is located.

title: Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property
content:
Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Nevada

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Nevada House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Nevada?
We buy Nevada houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How do Nevada's estate size tiers decide the probate route?

Nevada uses four routes, and the value of the estate and the presence of real property decide which one fits. Because a house is real property, most inherited homes cannot use the simple affidavit route.

RouteLimitKey conditionStatute
Affidavit for transfer$150,000 for a surviving spouse, $25,000 for any other claimantDecedent left no real property in Nevada; 40 days after deathNRS 146.080
Set aside without administrationEstate of $150,000 or lessCourt petition; may not begin until 30 days after deathNRS 146.070
Summary administrationGross value after encumbrances of $500,000 or lessCourt may order it if advisableNRS 145.040
Regular administrationAbove those limitsFull court supervisionNRS Title 12

The $500,000 figure comes from the current text of chapter 145, which the Legislature amended in 2025. Older web copies of the statute still show $300,000, so check the date on any source you rely on.

Value in the set-aside route is fair market value minus enforceable liens and encumbrances, measured as of the date of death, so a mortgage on the house reduces the number that counts.

Can heirs sell an inherited house in Nevada before probate ends?

Usually the person with authority to sell is the personal representative, who gets that authority from the court. The affidavit route in NRS 146.080 is closed whenever the decedent left real property or an interest in it, or a mortgage or lien on it, in Nevada, so a house generally goes through a court process or passes by a recorded deed.

A deed recorded before the owner's death that takes effect on death is the exception, and the Department of Taxation's transfer tax exemption list cites NRS 111.109 for it. For a house with no such deed, a petition for letters is the usual first step, and the petition must list the property, the heirs and devisees and whether the proposed representative has been convicted of a felony, as NRS 145.020 describes for summary cases.

Co-heirs should agree early on who will serve and on whether to sell or keep the house. A disagreement can slow the petition, and a creditor or an interested person can object to a sale at the confirmation hearing.

What does court confirmation of a sale involve?

In a supervised estate, a sale of real property generally has to be reported to the court and confirmed before title passes. NRS 148.060 requires the report and petition for confirmation within 30 days after the sale, and the clerk sets the matter for hearing with notice under NRS 155.010. Summary administration follows chapter 148 notice rules for real property sales under NRS 145.070.

The steps and safeguards that matter most:

  • Appraisal. A private sale cannot be confirmed unless the court is satisfied the price is fair market value and the property was appraised within 1 year before the sale. The court can waive the appraisal, for example when the sole heir is the representative, or when all devisees or heirs consent in writing, in which case assessed value can support confirmation (NRS 148.260).
  • Notice of sale. Notice is published in a county newspaper for 2 weeks, three publications a week apart, and the court may cut that for good cause to not less than 8 days. It may waive publication when the right people consent in writing, or when the property was publicly listed for at least 30 days (NRS 148.220).
  • Objections and higher bids. An interested person may file written objections, and other bidders may offer more when an offer is presented, in which case the court may confirm the highest bid (NRS 148.070, 148.120).
  • Commission. A broker's commission must be allowed by the court and cannot exceed 7 percent for improved real property or 10 percent for unimproved (NRS 148.110).

A private sale notice must state where offers are received and a day on or after which the sale will be made, at least 2 weeks after first publication unless the court shortens it, and the sale must happen within 1 year (NRS 148.240).

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What changes with independent administration?

A personal representative granted full authority under the Independent Administration of Estates Act can sell estate property without the usual confirmation steps. NRS 143.380 says the representative may sell at public auction or private sale, with or without notice, for cash or on credit, on terms the representative decides, and the confirmation requirements do not apply.

There is a safeguard tied to price. If the representative determines the real property will sell for less than 90 percent of its appraised value, all interested persons must consent in writing before the sale proceeds, and the sale must be confirmed by the court. The statute lists what confirmation looks at, including notice, the court's approval of commissions, the necessity of the sale and the effort to get the highest and best price reasonably attainable.

Independent administration can remove the confirmation step, but only if the will or the court allows the representative full authority. The statute also says the will can restrict those powers.

How do creditors and the family affect the sale?

Creditors get a window to file claims, and the surviving family can have a right to the home. In a summary administration, the representative publishes and mails notice to creditors, and creditors must file claims within 60 days after mailing or first publication, after which the representative has 15 days to allow or reject each claim under NRS 145.060. A claim not filed in time is barred, with an exception when the claimant did not get proper notice.

The family has separate protections. Under NRS 146.010, a surviving spouse or minor child is entitled to remain in possession of the homestead and to a reasonable provision for support. NRS 146.020 lets the court set apart the homestead, and property set apart is not subject to administration. A homestead selected and recorded by spouses during the marriage vests in the survivor under NRS 146.050.

A representative must close an estate within 18 months after appointment, with exceptions for pending claims, will contests and unresolved tax amounts under NRS 143.037.

What disclosure and tax rules apply when an estate sells a house?

The seller's 10 day disclosure form requirement does not apply to a fiduciary who takes temporary possession or title solely to facilitate a sale for a person who is deceased or incapacitated. NRS 113.130 lists personal representatives, guardians, trustees and agents under a power of attorney in that exception.

The transfer tax and property tax still matter. The county recorder collects the real property transfer tax when the deed is recorded, at $1.95 per $500 of value in most counties, according to the Nevada Department of Taxation. The Department also lists an exemption for a deed that becomes effective on the grantor's death under NRS 111.109. A Declaration of Value accompanies each deed.

Property tax keeps running while the estate is open. Installments are due on the third Monday of August and the first Mondays of October, January and March. In Clark County, the Assessor says any recorded ownership document removes the owner-occupied 3 percent abatement until a new postcard is returned, which is worth knowing for an heir who plans to live in the house.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How does a cash sale fit into a Nevada probate?

A cash buyer can purchase from the personal representative like any other buyer, and the court rules above still decide what approval is needed. In a supervised estate, the statute says a broker contract creates no liability for the estate unless a sale is made and confirmed by the court (NRS 148.110).

Questions to settle before accepting any offer:

  • Has the court issued letters, and does the representative have independent or supervised authority?
  • Is an appraisal on file within the last year, or will the heirs consent in writing to waive it?
  • Do the liens, taxes and creditor claims leave enough for the heirs after payoff?
  • Will the family keep any right to occupy the homestead until the closing?

We buy houses in Nevada as-is, and an estate sale is one of the situations we see. Terms depend on the property and the court process, and nothing here is a promise of a price. A Nevada probate attorney should review the specific steps for your case.

More questions about Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in Nevada?

Often yes. The affidavit route in NRS 146.080 is not available when the decedent left real property in Nevada. A house usually passes by a recorded deed that takes effect on death, or through a court-supervised estate with a personal representative.

What is the small estate limit in Nevada?

An estate of $150,000 or less can be set aside without administration by court order under NRS 146.070. The affidavit route allows $150,000 for a surviving spouse and $25,000 for any other claimant, but only with no real property.

How large an estate can use summary administration?

NRS 145.040 allows summary administration when the gross value of the estate after deducting encumbrances does not exceed $500,000, at the court's discretion. If the value is later found to exceed that amount, the representative must petition to revoke it.

Does the court have to approve the sale of estate real property?

In a supervised estate, generally yes. NRS 148.060 requires a report and a petition for confirmation within 30 days after the sale. With full authority under independent administration, confirmation is not required unless the price falls below 90 percent of appraised value.

How long do creditors have to file claims?

In a summary administration, creditors have 60 days after notice is mailed or first published to file, and the representative has 15 days after that to allow or reject each claim, under NRS 145.060.

How long can an estate stay open?

A personal representative must close the estate within 18 months after appointment under NRS 143.037, unless a claim in litigation, a will contest or an undetermined tax amount allows a court order to keep part of the estate open.
